zebralogic.title: Interpret adjacency and ordering clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: When a clue says 'directly left of', 'directly right of', or similar, enforce that the two houses are immediate neighbors; when it says 'somewhere left of' or 'somewhere right of', enforce only a strict ordering without requiring adjacency.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue contains spatial relationship terms such as 'directly left of', 'directly right of', 'somewhere left of', 'somewhere right of', or 'next to each other'.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'directly left of' as just 'left of' and allowing another house between the two items.

zebralogic.title: Interpret distance clues correctly
zebralogic.principle: A clue of the form 'N houses between X and Y' means there are exactly N houses separating X and Y, i.e., the distance between their positions is N+1.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue mentions a numeric distance between two entities.
zebralogic.example: Interpreting '2 houses between X and Y' as X being two houses away from Y (three positions apart) instead of having exactly two houses in between.

zebralogic.title: Treat 'somewhere left/right of' as inequality
zebralogic.principle: Clues like 'X is somewhere left of Y' impose only a strict ordering (pos(X) < pos(Y)), not adjacency; X and Y can be any distance apart as long as X is to the left of Y.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase 'somewhere left of' or 'somewhere right of'.
zebralogic.example: Assuming X must be immediately left of Y when the clue only says 'somewhere left of'.

zebralogic.title: Apply exclusion constraints
zebralogic.principle: If a clue explicitly forbids an attribute from a particular house (e.g., 'X is not in house 2'), enforce that the attribute cannot be placed in that house.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue contains a negative placement such as 'not in house N' or 'cannot be ...'.
zebralogic.example: Placing a person in a house that a clue explicitly says they are not in.

zebralogic.title: Enforce uniqueness across each attribute category
zebralogic.principle: Each value in a category must appear exactly once across all houses; no two houses can share the same attribute value.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: After any assignment, check that no attribute value is duplicated in the same category.
zebralogic.example: Assigning the same hobby to two different houses.

zebralogic.title: Preserve original case of attribute values
zebralogic.principle: When outputting the final grid, copy each attribute value exactly as it appears in the problem statement, preserving case, spelling, and any abbreviations.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During the final answer generation, before printing the grid.
zebralogic.example: Changing 'Blue Master' to 'blue master' or 'Blue master'.

zebralogic.title: Interpret 'next to each other' as adjacency
zebralogic.principle: Clues stating that X and Y are 'next to each other' mean their house positions differ by exactly one.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: When a clue uses the phrase 'next to each other' or similar.
zebralogic.example: Treating 'next to each other' as a non‑adjacent ordering, allowing a house between them.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for name-attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue directly links a specific name to an attribute (e.g., 'Alice is the doctor'), enforce both directions: the name has that attribute and that attribute belongs to that name.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue explicitly ties a name to an attribute.
zebralogic.example: Setting Alice = doctor but allowing another person also to be doctor.

zebralogic.title: Bidirectional equivalence for attribute-attribute clues
zebralogic.principle: When a clue links two non‑name attributes (e.g., 'The Norwegian uses a Samsung'), enforce that they belong to the same house in both directions.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: Whenever a clue ties two attribute values together.
zebralogic.example: Linking 'Swimmer' to 'high school' but not ensuring that the high‑school graduate is the swimmer.

zebralogic.title: Preserve exact attribute tokens (spelling, abbreviations) in output
zebralogic.principle: Use the attribute strings exactly as they appear in the problem definition, including any abbreviations, punctuation, or spelling; never substitute a synonym or shorten a term.
zebralogic.when_to_apply: During final answer construction, for each cell copy the token from the problem's attribute list.
zebralogic.example: Outputting 'apr' instead of the required 'april' or 'pall master' instead of 'pall mall'.

zebralogic.description: Interpreting 'N houses between' as distance N
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model treats the phrase as a simple offset rather than counting the houses that separate the two items, leading to off‑by‑one errors.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Translate 'N houses between X and Y' into the constraint |pos(X) - pos(Y)| = N + 1.

zebralogic.description: Ignoring equivalence clues that bind two attributes to the same house
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model records only a one‑way link, forgetting that the two attributes must co‑occur in the same house.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: When a clue states 'X is Y', enforce a bidirectional equivalence so both attributes point to the same house.

zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model may assign the same value to multiple houses because it does not keep a global uniqueness check.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: After each assignment, verify that each attribute value appears exactly once across all houses.

zebralogic.description: Altering attribute values (spelling/casing) instead of copying them verbatim
zebralogic.why_it_happens: The model normalises or abbreviates strings, assuming they are interchangeable, which changes the required output.
zebralogic.how_to_avoid: Copy attribute values directly from the problem statement without any modification.
